Ok, I think I got an intuition on the PageRank stuff:

  1. We imagine the internet as 3 websites
  2. User click links to other pages. They then land on other web pages

We can model this in aggregate as:

  1. A data structure holding how many % of web users are currently on which page (A, B or C)
  2. A matrix holding the chance that an average user will use from a specific page to a specific page (for example: Users on page A have a 34% chance to go to page B)

We also assume, for simplicity, that we have discrete time steps (let's say "once a minute") where every user clicks on a link to go to the next page, according to the stochastical "rules" of where you will go when you are e.g. on page A.

As the number of people in our model scales toward infinity, statistical noise cancels out. Instead of modeling individuals hopping from page to page following a weighted die, we simply talk about which percentage of overall users is on which page at a given timestep, and we analyze which percentage of these goes to which page at the time step, and assume this as constant. I think that falls under Law of Large Numbers but don't quote me on this.

We are now getting close to the relevant math, but we quickly have to get back to the actual use case: We are the early Google PageRank team, and we want to know which websites are important, to show them to people more often. In our model, we can clearly see which websites have how many visitors. Why aren't we just using these data? Answer, as I understand it:

  1. Google, neither then nor now, can't actually get a snapshot of where every internet user is right now
  2. Even if they could, the internet is very dynamic, with paged being born and dying, so nothing would "settle"

As such, the idea of original PageRank, as I understand it is:

They made up heuristics on how users move through the web. Originally, they did this via just statically analyzing how many links on which website point to which other websites. You can then build a graph just like above, taking informed guesses on what the "chance that the user will go from a.com to b.org" is, instead of just making up values like we did.

You can then run a simulation (like we did, but a tiny bit more complex, because there are more than three web pages) and let the simulated people move around and simply wait until it's settled. You have then, actually found the eigenvector in this context:

The eigenvector in the PageRank context is the vector describing the percentage of people on all websites that does not change when we move people around at the next timestep according to the guessed rules of the percentages of people moving from website to website.

In other words, you run the simulation that we just ran, wait for it to be settled, you take your distribution of people over all websites, and that's your eigenvector.

Meaning, we can just read our eigenvector from the simulation:

[0.213, 0.346, 0.441]

...which stand for the percentage of people on a.com, b.org and c.io, respectively.

Its eigenvalue is 1, which means that "nothing moves".

== Trying to get eigenvalues and Schrödinger to meet

So where do eigenvalues and Schrödinger meet?

OK so apparently "eigenvalue equation" is a general term, describing a class of equations in linear algebra, in general.

They always mean that you apply a matrix to a vector, and you get back the same vector, multiplied by a scaling factor (which is the eigenvalue). PageRank notwithstanding, this gives me almost nothing understanding-wise.

I mean maybe this isn't terribly important but not understanding the overall shape of an equation this short feels not-good.

Maybe we can grasp the gestalt with some more examples.
Going back to PageRank, we would (I think/Gemini says) just state a very prototypical eigenvalue equation:

M𝐫=λ𝐫

Because we want an eigenvector where nothing changes, we want the eigenvalue to be 1, thus the equation simplifies to

M𝐫=𝐫

...which stands for "what's the people-distribution-vector (r) that we can multiply with our what-percentage-goes-where matrix such that it does not change".

OK. Perhaps we can accept that eigenvalue equations just state the desire or fact that some scenario behaves like that.

Apparently in the Schrödinger then, two things "do not change at all": the probability distribution, which somehow describes where the electron of an atom sort of statistically is, and the "energy value".
